content: Recreational water, such as open water sources, can become contaminated with feces from waterfowl. Infected birds can excrete significant amounts of influenza virus in their feces. Influenza viruses can survive in feces for up to four weeks, with survival duration influenced by environmental factors such as pH and temperature. The disposal of dead infected animals and potentially contaminated solid waste must be conducted appropriately by trained personnel, adhering to local regulations. Monitoring the health of individuals exposed to animals infected with influenza or those in contact with individuals with zoonotic influenza is critical. Enhanced surveillance and awareness of zoonotic influenza should be prioritized. Coordination and information exchange between animal health and public health sectors are essential for effective response efforts, following the One Health approach. All suspected cases of zoonotic influenza should be investigated to provide appropriate treatment, identify and monitor potential human contacts, and assess whether human-to-human transmission is occurring. If a person is suspected of having zoonotic influenza, health authorities must be notified, and clinical case management should include testing, triage, disease severity assessment, risk factor evaluation, isolation, and treatment with antivirals and supportive care. Laboratory-confirmed cases must be reported to the World Health Organization (WHO) under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), and public health authorities should initiate contact tracing and risk assessment. Public health and animal health authorities should collaborate during investigations of human cases of zoonotic influenza. Genetic information on viruses from animals and humans is crucial for risk assessment. Surveillance should include active screening in hospitals, engagement with private practitioners and diagnostic laboratories, and monitoring of high-risk occupational groups, such as healthcare workers and individuals exposed to live or dead animals. Those exposed to infected animals or farms under suspicion should be registered and closely monitored by local health authorities to enable early detection of illness and timely clinical management. Testing of asymptomatic exposed individuals may be considered on a case-by-case basis, depending on resources and objectives, such as outbreak investigations or studies on asymptomatic transmission. The collection of diagnostic specimens from suspected human cases is essential for early detection, patient management, public health risk assessment, and response planning. Specimens should be collected safely using appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) and transported correctly. Preferred specimens include upper and lower respiratory tract samples, as well as blood for serum collection. Laboratories must be capable of processing and confirming human infections with animal influenza viruses, and virus sharing with WHO Collaborating Centres is vital for monitoring viral evolution and updating diagnostics and vaccines. Healthcare facilities must be prepared to manage patients with zoonotic influenza. This includes raising awareness among healthcare workers, screening and triaging patients, and using appropriate precautions such as droplet and airborne precautions during aerosol-generating procedures. Healthcare workers should be monitored for symptoms, provided with PPE, and trained in its use. Clinical management of influenza patients should aim to prevent severe illness and death. For patients with confirmed or suspected influenza virus infection, early treatment with oseltamivir is recommended, especially for those with severe or progressive illness or at increased risk of severe disease. Empiric treatment should not be delayed if laboratory results are pending. Corticosteroids should not be used routinely but may be considered in specific cases, such as septic shock or co-infection with SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics should only be used if bacterial co-infection is suspected, and their use should be discontinued if microbiological findings are negative. Optimized supportive care, including oxygen therapy and advanced respiratory support, is essential for patients with severe influenza. Lung-protective ventilation strategies should be followed for those requiring mechanical ventilation. All laboratory-confirmed cases of zoonotic influenza must be reported to WHO under the IHR (2005). While seasonal influenza vaccines do not protect against animal influenza A viruses, they may reduce the likelihood of co-infections and the emergence of pandemic strains. Vaccines against zoonotic influenza viruses, such as A(H5N1), have been developed and licensed in some countries but are not widely available. Pandemic influenza vaccines can only be produced once the specific pandemic strain is identified, with the first doses available 4–6 months after identification.
